extracted.intended_audience: students and instructors of algebraic geometry (graduate-level or advanced undergraduates)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and pedagogical standards for using, teaching from, and learning the textbook 'The Rising Sea: Foundations of Algebraic Geometry' (Vakil). Covers prerequisites, structure, reading order, exercise usage, level-of-generality choices, and conventions for a first-year graduate (or rigorous first) course in algebraic geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: This book has a lot of exercises; exercises are interspersed with the exposition rather than left to the end, and most have been extensively field-tested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "I have found that unless I have some problems I can think through, ideas don’t get fixed in my mind." Work through a significant number of exercises — some are trivial, some experts may find them offensive, a few are hard but intended given background. Hints may help but sometimes they may not. (See 0.0.1 and 0.0.1 repeated admonition about working exercises.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure and numbering conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything is numbered by chapter and section, and the same numbering continues throughout; individual paragraphs often get numbers; definitions are in bold; exercises are indicated by letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is done "for ease of reference." Expect a disciplined, reference-friendly layout suitable for course use and citation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep geometric motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: When introduced to a new idea, always ask why you should care and try to apply any new abstraction to a concrete example you can understand well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Do not be seduced by the lotus-eaters into infatuation with untethered abstraction. Hold tight to your geometric motivation as you learn the formal structures..." Be patient: an immediate answer may not appear, but demand one eventually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended reading order / logical dependencies
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a recommended sequence of chapters (Figure 0.1) showing logical dependences: start with category theory and sheaves, then schemes (Chapters 3–5), morphisms (6–10), dimension and smoothness (11–12), quasicoherent sheaves and cohomology (13–21), advanced tools (23–30).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the dependency graph for which chapters should be read before others, but "taken with a grain of salt" — some flexibility is acceptable depending on goals and prior knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category theory early
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter 1 on category theory is presented as language with embedded logic; it prepares readers to think cleanly about later material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Category theory should not be skipped — understand concepts like cokernel, product, and Yoneda’s Lemma to benefit later exposition. "Yoneda’s Lemma — and more generally, the idea of understanding an object through the maps to it — will play an important role."

rubrics_metrics.name: Sheaves early
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter 2 (sheaves) is treated early to package and work with local information effectively (stalks, sheafification, sheaves on a base).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sheaf theory abstracts familiar ideas (motivating example: sheaf of differentiable functions); understand how best to package sheaf information since later chapters rely on it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor adaptation and course design
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructors should adapt the book to their own point of view and course goals, choosing an application or theorem to reach as the course target and pacing accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "If you use this book for a course, you should of course adapt it to your own point of view and your own interests." Use Figure 0.1 to map out a course; it is better to take more time and end at the right place for students than to sprint to the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of exposition when two approaches exist
rubrics_metrics.description: When there are two approaches and one is 'correct' from an advanced viewpoint but the other is direct and natural from a naive viewpoint, the book chooses the latter for learners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Decisions on how to describe things were made for the sake of the learners." This is an explicit pedagogical principle: favor clarity and directness for learners over maximal generality in exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality principle
rubrics_metrics.description: State results in the maximal generality that the proof justifies, but do not give a much harder proof if the stronger generality will not be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the weakest hypotheses necessary to prove a result clearly; include extra generality only when it clarifies or will be used later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noetherian hypotheses: use sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Noetherian hypotheses are handy when necessary but otherwise misleading; restrict to Noetherian cases only when needed (or when it saves effort).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out Noetherian assumptions only when used in proofs so readers understand when the property matters. Introduce quasiseparatedness early as a preferable hypothesis in many places.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment choice for cohomology
rubrics_metrics.description: Cohomology is taught first using the Čech approach (as Serre did), with derived functor cohomology introduced later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ordering is chosen to be pedagogically accessible: introduce Čech cohomology to build intuition before derived functors, even though Grothendieck viewed the agreement as 'accidental.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize examples and pathologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Pathological examples are useful warning signs and reality checks; the book includes many examples (e.g., curves, 27 lines on cubic) to consolidate understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use classical and pathological examples to test new theorems and to understand which hypotheses are necessary (likened to roadside markers on mountain highways).

rubrics_metrics.name: Starred sections as reading guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections are marked with stars: ⋆ (starred) are optional and worth knowing on a second/third reading; ⋆⋆ (double-starred) should not be read on a first pass unless you really want to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Starred sections are not necessarily harder, merely unimportant. You should not read double-starred sections (⋆⋆) unless you really really want to, but you should be aware of their existence." Use the star system to prioritize reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background prerequisites and conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers are expected to know basic commutative ring theory (ideals, localization), tensor products, exact sequences, some field theory, and basic topology; rings are assumed commutative with 1, and the Axiom of Choice is accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplementary references are recommended for background (Eisenbud, Atiyah–Macdonald, Matsumura, Weibel, Stacks project). The reader should be familiar with topology and other mathematical areas for intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of working with peers / instructors
rubrics_metrics.description: The book is usable for self-study but most learners benefit greatly from group study or someone to ask questions of; instructors should provide context and adaptations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Most mortals cannot learn algebraic geometry fully on their own; ideally you should read in a group, and even if not, you should have someone you can ask questions to (both stupid and smart questions)."

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on minimal useful hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor hypotheses that make proofs cleaner and more memorable, but avoid unnecessary ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reasonable hypothesis simplifies the proof and aids memory, include it; but avoid hypotheses that are not used in the proof (they are red herrings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Line bundles prioritized over general Cartier divisors
rubrics_metrics.description: The exposition treats line bundles (maps to projective space) as more fundamental than divisors; general Cartier divisors are not discussed except where necessary (effective Cartier divisors play a role).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedagogical choice: emphasize notions that are conceptually and technically most useful for the intended audience, even if classical texts emphasize divisors earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the book as core of a one-year rigorous course
rubrics_metrics.description: The core material is intended to be digestible over a single year, giving students a broad familiarity with foundations and preparing them for seminars and further study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course planners should choose essential topics and accept that the book is challenging but designed to leave students ready to learn advanced material after a year of study.
